title: I spent $4,000 on a robot dog from China
gist: A first-person review of a $4,017 Unitree Go2 Pro quadruped becomes a cost-curve analysis: Unitree's cheapest Go2 Air is more than 97 percent below Boston Dynamics' $75,000 Spot, achieved through identical reusable motors, deliberately lower-quality components, field-serviceable legs, and a 6.33:1 gearbox paired with oversized motors instead of expensive 51:1 reducers. Unitree's humanoid revenue grew eightfold to RMB 867 million in 2025 and now exceeds half of company revenue, its Shanghai IPO on August 19 rose more than fivefold on day one to a $34 billion valuation, and the author argues US import restrictions may simply cede the global market the way EV policy did to BYD.

themes.theme: Price collapse as the real technology event

insights.claim: The author paid $4,017 after tariffs and shipping for a Unitree Go2 Pro, versus around $15,000 for the research-grade Unitree quadrupeds in a George Mason University lab and roughly $75,000 starting price for Boston Dynamics' Spot.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: An order-of-magnitude price gap against the Western incumbent is the entire competitive story in legged robotics right now.
insights.locator: But my robot did have one big thing going for it

insights.claim: Unitree's cheapest robot, the Go2 Air, is more than 97 percent cheaper than Spot, though the author notes this is not apples-to-apples since Spot is larger and carries heavier payloads.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Even discounted for capability differences, the price delta redefines who can buy a legged robot, which is what expands the market.
insights.locator: Today, Unitree’s cheapest robot

insights.claim: Unitree's pricing ladder fell fast: Laikago in 2017 and AlienGo in 2019 cost tens of thousands of dollars, the 2021 Go1 Air started at $2,700, and the 2023 Go2 was $1,600 for Air and $2,800 for Pro.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A documented four-generation cost curve gives a rate of decline to extrapolate onto humanoid pricing.
insights.locator: That created an opening for Unitree

insights.claim: The author's framing is that what changes the world is often not inventing a technology but making it affordable for a mass market, citing Xerox inventing the GUI personal computer while Apple, IBM and Microsoft made it mainstream.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Directs attention away from capability demos toward unit cost and volume as the variables that determine who wins a hardware category.
insights.quote: Sometimes what changes the world isn’t the invention of a new technology; it’s figuring out how to make it affordable enough for a mass market.
insights.locator: But my robot did have one big thing going for it

insights.claim: The author is candid that the robot is useful for very little: wheeled robots are faster and more energy-efficient for delivery, flying drones are better for survey and inspection, and the quadruped has no arms or hands so it is mostly useless around the house.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Demand for quadrupeds is not yet application-driven, so revenue growth depends on research, entertainment and price-discovery buyers rather than proven ROI.
insights.locator: Several people have asked me what my robot

insights.claim: The product has visible rough edges: a buggy control app, stair climbing and human-following that do not work well in real life, legs that thrash if the robot starts up misaligned, and a walk home that ended with the robot collapsing onto its back at 5 percent battery and 84 degrees Celsius internal temperature without a graceful shutdown.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Polish is being traded away for cost, the same tradeoff early DJI made, so product-quality critiques may not predict competitive outcomes.
insights.locator: Like DJI in 2013, Unitree’s robots today

themes.theme: Engineering choices behind the cost structure

insights.claim: Each Unitree leg uses three motors (one shoulder, one per leg segment) and all motors are identical throughout the robot, with a Simplexity engineer noting reduced cost, reduced part count and greater robustness from reuse.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Part-count reduction through motor standardization is the transferable manufacturing lesson and a benchmark for evaluating competing robot BOMs.
insights.quote: They use all the same motors throughout
insights.locator: Why are Unitree robots so cheap?

insights.claim: A motors and legged-robot expert at MAB Robotics argues Unitree also saved money using low-quality components, with its largely in-house motors wearing out faster than those in some other robot brands.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Durability, not headline price, is where the hidden total-cost-of-ownership risk sits for institutional buyers of Chinese robots.
insights.locator: Jakub Bartoszek, an expert on motors

insights.claim: Unitree designed legs to be field-serviceable, with a Simplexity engineer estimating a leg swap takes less than a minute thanks to how simply legs attach to the body.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Designing for cheap repair converts a durability weakness into an acceptable operating model, which is how low-cost hardware survives in the field.
insights.locator: Unitree seems to have designed its robots

insights.claim: Unitree pairs large powerful motors with a simple 6.33-to-1 gearbox instead of the expensive high-ratio reducers used elsewhere, where Boston Dynamics' Spot uses 51-to-1 gear ratios in two leg motors.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The reducer is the expensive component; designing it out is the single largest identified cost lever in legged robot BOMs.
insights.locator: How powerful motors enable cheap actuators

insights.claim: Low gear ratios improve backdriveability and electrical sensing of physical resistance, make robots more nimble and dynamic, and make the design easier to simulate and therefore easier to train.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The cost-saving choice also improves trainability, meaning cheap hardware compounds with better learned control rather than trading against it.
insights.locator: In contrast, Unitree uses large motors

insights.claim: The shift to lower gear ratios is an industry-wide trend because modern robots perform complex actions in unpredictable environments where sophisticated control software makes constant small corrections and can compensate for less precise hardware.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Software is substituting for mechanical precision across robotics, which structurally favors companies strong in control learning over precision-machining incumbents.
insights.locator: Unitree’s decision to use a lower gear ratio

insights.claim: Unitree receives significant Chinese government support including tax credits and large-scale purchases by public institutions, which the author says clearly helped it scale manufacturing and drive down per-unit cost even though the scale is hard to quantify.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: State-backed demand plus tax support is part of the cost advantage, which is the substantive basis for Western trade-policy arguments.
insights.locator: Unitree also gets significant support

insights.claim: Unitree's quadruped revenue tripled between 2024 and 2025 from RMB 230 million ($34 million) to RMB 697 million ($104 million), while humanoid revenue rose eightfold from RMB 107 million ($16 million) to RMB 867 million ($129 million) per filings tied to its August stock offering.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Humanoids are growing nearly three times faster than quadrupeds off a similar base, the clearest financial evidence that the humanoid market is real.
insights.locator: According to filings connected to Unitree’s August stock offering

insights.claim: Humanoids accounted for 51 percent of Unitree's revenue in 2025, and the author expects the figure to be higher for 2026.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Unitree has already crossed from being a quadruped company to a humanoid company, which is how it should be valued and benchmarked.
insights.locator: Humanoids accounted for 51 percent

insights.claim: Unitree debuted on the Shanghai stock market on August 19 with shares rising more than fivefold on the first day, and at Monday's close was still valued at $34 billion, more than triple its pre-IPO valuation.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A $34 billion public valuation on roughly RMB 1.5 billion of combined 2025 revenue sets an extreme multiple that anchors comparable humanoid-robotics valuations globally.
insights.locator: Financial markets are bullish

insights.claim: Unitree sells humanoid robots for as little as $13,500 for the consumer G1, with a research-grade EDU version costing around $50,000, versus humanoids that were dramatically more expensive a few years ago.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A $13,500 humanoid resets the price expectation that Western humanoid startups must eventually meet or beat.
insights.locator: The humanoid pivot

insights.claim: A humanoid is materially harder than a quadruped: the Go2 has 12 motors total while the cheapest G1 has 23 (five per arm, six per leg, one torso) and its leg motors must be more powerful because balancing on two legs is more work than standing on four.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Roughly double the actuator count plus higher power means humanoid unit economics improve more slowly than quadruped economics did.
insights.locator: A humanoid robot is more than a quadruped

insights.claim: Unitree's quadruped business gave it a head start in humanoids through years of shipping experience, deep actuator design expertise and an extensive supplier network by the early 2020s.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Supplier networks and actuator know-how, not algorithms, are the transferable asset between robot form factors, which favors incumbents with shipped volume.
insights.locator: Still, I suspect that Unitree’s experience

themes.theme: The DJI analogy and the vertical-integration flywheel

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis wrote in June that we are witnessing the birth of another Chinese hardware giant, noting Unitree parlayed quadruped dominance into creating and leading the humanoid market within about three years.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Third-party analyst conviction that Unitree follows the DJI trajectory is the framing most likely to drive capital allocation in the sector.
insights.quote: We are witnessing the birth of another Chinese hardware giant
insights.locator: Unitree could have a durable advantage

insights.claim: The flywheel argument is that higher unit volume yields better supplier terms and more capital for manufacturing optimization and in-housing components, which pushes costs lower and drives more sales, the mechanism by which DJI came to dominate global drones.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing cost-volume loop means market position compounds and late entrants face a widening, not closing, gap.
insights.locator: There’s a flywheel here

insights.claim: Unitree has developed its own motors, gearboxes, lidar sensors and cameras, with SemiAnalysis reporting its self-produced motors can run as low as 30 to 40 percent of the cost of equivalent Western motors and that it makes some of the cheapest humanoid gearboxes in the world.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A 60 to 70 percent cost advantage on the dominant BOM component is the specific, quantified moat Western robot makers must overcome.
insights.quote: Unitree’s self-produced motors can run as low as 30-40% of equivalent Western motors
insights.locator: According to SemiAnalysis, Unitree has developed

insights.claim: The DJI precedent is that the Phantom 1 shipped in January 2013 at $679 with no built-in camera, no gimbal, ten minutes of flight and no live video, but at roughly half the cost of a build-it-yourself drone, and DJI in-housed the flight controller first then gimbals, motors and ESCs.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Sequencing matters: in-house the most expensive, technically hardest component first, the playbook to watch Unitree execute in humanoids.
insights.locator: The SemiAnalysis authors draw a parallel to DJI

insights.claim: DJI's cost reduction unlocked entirely new markets that were previously the domain of helicopters and Hollywood second-unit teams, including real estate listings, wedding videos, local news and agricultural surveying.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The analogy implies the useful robot applications do not exist yet and will be created by the price point, so current lack of use cases is not disqualifying.
insights.locator: Before DJI came along

insights.claim: Unitree is the global leader in quadrupeds but Chinese rival AgiBot has sold more humanoid robots than Unitree in recent months, with many smaller Chinese robot companies able to challenge both in coming years.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The humanoid leadership claim is already contested inside China, tempering the winner-take-all read on Unitree's valuation.
insights.locator: Of course that’s not guaranteed to happen

insights.claim: Unitree faces little competition in the US or the West: Boston Dynamics sells excellent but significantly more expensive robots, and American humanoid efforts including Tesla, Figure and 1X do not sell a robot consumers can buy today.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: No Western vendor is currently contesting the consumer and research price tiers, so restrictions create a supply vacuum rather than shifting demand.
insights.locator: But Unitree does not face much competition

insights.claim: A bipartisan House group introduced a bill in June to restrict importation of Chinese robots with Unitree named in the official press release, and in July the FCC imposed broad new regulations on foreign-made robots likely to affect Unitree and other Chinese companies.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Regulatory action is already in motion and names the company directly, a concrete market-access risk for anyone building on Unitree hardware.
insights.locator: That has alarmed some American policymakers

insights.claim: The author argues the robot market is global, so even if Chinese companies are locked out of the US, Unitree or a Chinese rival could still dominate worldwide, drawing a parallel to BYD and electric vehicles, and warns a ban could make the US a robotics backwater rather than hampering Unitree.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The EV precedent suggests protection without domestic cost competitiveness produces isolation, not catch-up, the key risk for US robotics policy and investment.
insights.quote: rather than hampering the growth of companies like Unitree, it could make the US a robotics backwater
insights.locator: There’s an obvious parallel here to electric vehicles

insights.claim: Unitree founder Wang Xingxing built a crude quadruped called XDog for his master's thesis at Shanghai University, cited Boston Dynamics' Marc Raibert as his idol in a 2016 interview, and stated his goal was to make quadrupeds simpler and smaller so they could help ordinary people.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The cost-down strategy was the founding thesis, not a later pivot, which supports the claim that it is durable rather than opportunistic.
insights.quote: make quadruped robots simpler and smaller, so that they can help ordinary people with things like carrying objects or as companions
insights.locator: Unitree founder Wang Xingxing developed

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics unveiled its electric quadruped Spot in June 2016 but did not make it commercially available until 2020, creating an opening that Unitree, founded in May 2016, exploited with Laikago in 2017.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A four-year gap between demo and commercial availability is how the incumbent lost the category, a cautionary timeline for today's Western humanoid developers.
insights.locator: Boston Dynamics officially unveiled an electric quadruped

insights.claim: A George Mason University roboticist says that ten years ago only a very small set of research groups worked on quadruped locomotion because they were the only people who could build a quadruped, and that Unitree basically democratized the entire field.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Cheap hardware widened the research base, which accelerates the software and control advances that determine the next capability generation.
insights.quote: Then Unitree came onto the market. And it basically democratized the entire world of quadruped locomotion research.
insights.locator: How Unitree democratized legged robotics
